laws_treaties: Quo warranto procedure under the Rules of Court

stances.claim: The Court placed more value on procedural technicalities than on a substantive decision to free its own members from the risk of QW ouster and to restore impeachment as the only process to remove them — a missed opportunity for institutional self-defense.
stances.rhetorical_move: respectful-disagreement: doctrinal correction couched in deference
stances.evidence: The Court's short-shrift dismissal of the certiorari/MR on the same procedural grounds; ample 'transcendental importance' jurisprudence permitting waiver of procedural niceties

stances.claim: Republic v. Sereno was decided without Senate-style trial, by a simple 8-6 majority (CJ inhibited), and on grounds (SALN non-filing prior to incumbency) the Constitution does not authorize for justice removal — making it doctrinally suspect and vulnerable to future challenge.
stances.evidence: Constitution's silence on QW as a removal method; framers' non-discussion; vote breakdown and inhibition pattern

stances.claim: Impeachment is constitutionally and structurally more careful, cautious, and rigorous than QW: House Committee majority for sufficiency in form and substance; House plenary one-third for articles; Senate trial; two-thirds Senate concurrence (at least 16 of 24 senators) for conviction.
stances.rhetorical_move: process-comparison: rule-design argument from procedural rigor
stances.evidence: Step-by-step constitutional walkthrough of impeachment vs. QW vote requirements

stances.claim: At least three future pathways can return the QW-removal-method issue to the Court for merits resolution: a fresh procedurally-correct QW petition against an incumbent; a Sereno petition for restoration on void-ab-initio grounds; or congressional legislation repealing the QW doctrine.

stances.evidence: Constitutional separation-of-powers + jurisprudence-as-law theory + standing rules

stances.claim: Despite respectful disagreement with the Court, the verdict binds 'this ancient retiree (and everyone else for that matter)' — modeling civic acceptance of judicial supremacy even amid principled dissent.
stances.rhetorical_move: civic-finality acknowledgment paired with retained right to disagree
stances.evidence: Author's self-positioning as former CJ and present commentator; 'agree to disagree' aphorism

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban observes that the Supreme Court has effectively 'decided not to decide' the quo warranto (QW) issue hanging above the heads of its justices -- the 'sword of Damocles' from Republic v. Sereno (May 18, 2018). He recounts that in three earlier columns (April 18, May 16, June 6), he had urged the Court to use the Justice Edgardo L. delos Santos QW occasion to reverse that doctrine, restore the constitutional shroud of judicial independence, and re-establish impeachment as the exclusive removal process. The Court did treat the second certiorari petition as a motion for reconsideration of the dismissed QW petition (which had been thrown out on procedural errors -- wrong remedy, failure to pay docket fees, etc.) -- but then dismissed the MR on the same procedural grounds via 'short shrift,' placing more value on procedural technicalities than on a substantive resolution of judicial-independence. He maps three future pathways through which the issue can return for merits resolution: (1) a fresh, procedurally-correct QW petition against an incumbent SC member; (2) a petition by Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno to be restored on the ground that Republic v. Sereno was void ab initio for grave abuse of discretion and unconstitutionality; or (3) congressional legislation repealing the QW doctrine on the theory that jurisprudence forms part of the law of the land subject to legislative repeal, followed by judicial review of the new statute. He contrasts QW (majority vote of justices, no trial-type hearing) with the much more careful and rigorous constitutional impeachment process (House Committee on Justice majority for form/substance; House plenary one-third for articles; Senate trial; two-thirds Senate concurrence -- at least 16 of 24 senators -- for conviction), and reminds readers that Sereno was ousted 8-6 (with the CJ inhibited) on grounds the Constitution does not mention as a basis for justice removal. He closes by accepting the Court's verdict in the spirit of internal Court culture: 'we can agree to disagree without being disagreeable, and we can differ without being difficult.'
